strengths: The paper addresses a relevant robustness problem: learning one invariant cue may be insufficient when that cue disappears at test time. H-CMNIST provides a useful controlled diagnostic. In Table 1, ASGDRO improves shape-only accuracy from GDRO's 61.44±1.03% to 69.17±6.19%, supporting improved robustness to the tested feature removal.

The empirical evaluation spans subpopulation shifts, domain generalization, and WILDS/MetaShift. Table 2 reports improved worst-group accuracy over GDRO on all five datasets, including 68.6% to 74.2% on CMNIST and 87.2% to 90.0% on CelebA.

The controlled DPLCLIP comparisons provide useful evidence of practical value. With training-domain validation, ASGDRO improves average DomainBed accuracy from 75.8% to 77.5%, with improvements on all four datasets and a 3.7-point gain on TerraIncognita.

The optimizer is straightforward to integrate, combining adaptive sharpness-aware perturbations with group-loss reweighting. Algorithm 1 and the hyperparameter and model-selection details in Appendices A, B, and D provide a substantial basis for implementation.
weaknesses: The central explanation connecting flatness to sufficient invariant learning is not established. Section 3.1 assumes that parameter directions correspond to individual invariant features and that flatness indicates successful feature learning; changing the covariance of constructed Gaussian losses does not demonstrate acquisition of another feature. SIL also lacks an operational sufficiency criterion. The useful empirical gains balance against this unresolved central claim, placing the submission near the acceptance boundary.

The shared ERM-derived perturbation does not necessarily expose each group's sharp directions: average gradients can cancel or be dominated by majority groups. Thus, evaluating all groups at that perturbation does not establish minimization of their worst neighborhood losses. Section 3.3 provides no direct ablation against group-specific perturbations or a perturbation derived from the GDRO-weighted loss. These controls matter because the algorithmic contribution largely combines existing ASAM and GDRO components.

The mechanism analyses are suggestive rather than conclusive. Broader Grad-CAM activation does not establish reliance on multiple independently useful invariant cues. Likewise, Table 4 and Figure 6 compare raw Hessian eigenvalues without addressing the parameter-scale sensitivity that motivates ASAM in Section 3.2. Neither analysis establishes the claimed guarantee of sufficient feature learning.

Several performance comparisons are difficult to assess statistically. Table 2 imports most baseline results and omits variability despite reporting three-seed averages; the Waterbirds improvement over GDRO is only 0.4 points. Figure 4 also lacks uncertainty estimates, and Section 4.4 supplies insufficient training, tuning, and selection details for reproducing the WILDS/MetaShift results. These limitations weaken confidence in the magnitude and attribution of some gains.

There are correctable specification issues distinct from the main scientific concerns. Equation 1 writes a first-order perturbation approximation as an exact argmax equality. Appendix A.1 calls the CMNIST test correlation reversed, but describes class 0 as 80% red during training and 90% red during testing. The intended distribution needs clarification.
